articles.title: Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats
articles.summary: Early indications suggest it will be some time before the shape of new government and who will lead it is clear
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison in Tel Aviv Julian Borger in Jerusalem and Peter Beaumont

blocks.text: Israel’s election was too close to call on Tuesday night after a historic turnout by voters for an election described by some as the most consequential in the country’s history, and marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters.

Exit polls published on Tuesday evening, they suggested that the opposition bloc of parties led by the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin, edging out Benjamin Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition despite the prime minister’s Likud emerging as the largest party.
The result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called.

After a day in which Israelis streamed to polling stations across the country, exit polls suggested Netanyahu’s ability to command the loyalty of a large core of Likud party voters remained undimmed despite his rejection by large numbers of Israelis.

The predicted haul of up to 18 Knesset seats for Israeli Arab parties is likely to make them the kingmakers in what seem certain to be protracted talks to form a new government, with Netanyahu likely to fall short of the support required to form a new coalition.

The exit polls – if they prove accurate – suggest a struggle for either Likud or Eisenkot’s Yashar to find a road to a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Likud’s projected showing, not for the first time, appears to have defied predictions in the runup to the vote.
What is clear, however, is that Netanayhu no longer has a claim to a mandate with his political fate in the balance.

The exit polls were released after a last-ditch effort by Netanyahu and several other parties to keep polling stations open beyond their 10pm deadline was rejected by the Central Elections Committee as the prime minister suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee that said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.
Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.

Tuesday’s election, which drew the highest turnout in 50 years, had been framed as a referendum on nearly 17 years of unbroken rule by Benjamin Netanyahu, who has most recently overseen three years of unprecedented conflict, instability and growing international isolation.

With more than 7 million people eligible to vote, by 6pm voter turnout was 74.3% – a rise of about 9% on the previous election – with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting. There were also reports of tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad who had arrived to vote in recent days, with many still arriving at Ben Gurion airport to cast their ballots on Tuesday.

Voting was heavy in a number of major cities, including Tel Aviv and Haifa, which some analysts had suggested would benefit the opposition, with long queues to vote in some locations. That pattern was repeated in Israeli-Arab towns, many of which have a long history of boycotting elections.

blocks.caption: Israeli-Arab voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling station in Nazareth. Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: As polls opened on Tuesday, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition allies launched what critics condemned as a scare campaign to encourage their supporters to turn out, with the familiar racist tactic of warning that large numbers of Israeli Arabs would be voting. Netanyahu made a similar claim to rally support in 2015.

In a recorded message to voters, Netanyahu suggested Arabs and the left were trying to steal the election and Likud claimed suspected irregularities at hundreds of polling stations used by Israeli Arabs.
Israeli citizens of Palestinian origin make up about 20% of the country’s population.
That prompted Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, to say Netanyahu was laying the ground to challenge the result.

blocks.caption: A Likud election poster at a polling station in Jerusalem. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Netanyahu has returned to his familiar tricks, lies and fearmongering to mobilise voters,” he said. “The same lies we saw in previous election campaigns.”

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023 – an event that many blamed on Netanyahu’s failings – Israel has devastated Gaza with the loss of more than 74,000 Palestinian lives, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war with the US against Iran.

Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners have also attracted international opprobrium for Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank, where violent Jewish settlers have been accused of pogroms against Palestinians and ethnic cleansing.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian family walk past campaign posters for Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, in Beit Kahil in the West Bank. Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Despite the many issues confronting the country, much of the focus in the campaign has been on the contrasting characters of the two main party leaders – the machiavellian, grandstanding Netanyahu, who is on trial for corruption, against Eisenkot, the unpolished former IDF chief of staff who rose from humble origins.
The campaign, unusually febrile even by Israeli standards, included a struggling Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

On Tuesday, encouraging ultra-orthodox voters, Netanyahu – who has long elided his personal and political survival with that of Israel – returned to his apocalyptic language. “The Jewish state is on the brink of ruin,” he said.

In the midst of a major trial for corruption, which has been moving at a glacial pace through the courts, Netanyahu has appeared rattled by the challenge mounted against him by an array of centre-right parties whose unifying pitch has been “anyone but Netanyahu”.

“This is a very moving and fateful moment,” he told journalists after voting, saying he believed the Arab parties that could make or break the election were “receiving massive, truly massive, support ... heading to the polls in unprecedented numbers”.

Despite tonight’s results, the complexity of Israel’s fragmented political system, with many parties jostling and horse trading, means that it will probably be some time before the shape of any future government – and who will lead it – is clear.
All of which has amplified the importance of Israeli Arab parties, which could emerge as potential kingmakers.
“Our vote will change the government,” the head of the Islamist Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, said while voting, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.

Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for taunting Palestinian detainees and saying some Palestinians in Gaza are “not even people”, said “it will be Mansour Abbas’s government” if Netanyahu and his allies lose.
Underlining the sense of a country at a defining crossroads, an editorial in the left-leaning Haaretz publication had exhorted Israelis to vote which they did in huge numbers.

“Israel cannot afford another four years under Netanyahu,” it said. “It has exhausted its reserves. The erosion of its diplomatic credit has reached dangerous proportions, and its tired citizens are at the very limits of what they can bear.”

articles.title: U.S. and Cuban officials get into shouting match on floor of United Nations
articles.summary: U.S. and Cuban officials engaged in a stunning shouting match on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, the latest in a series of public spats between the longtime adversaries…

image.caption: UN officials tried to tone down outbursts Tuesday as the U.S. ambassador to the UN was speaking against Cuba and an annual resolution coming up for vote later this week. (UNTV/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. and Cuban officials engaged in a stunning shouting match on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, the latest in a series of public spats between the longtime adversaries over Washington's escalating economic campaign against Havana.
U.S. ambassador was urging vote against Cuban resolution prompting island delegation to call him a liar

The interaction began shortly after U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz took the podium to argue against supporting the annual resolution this week condemning the decades-long U.S. economic embargo against the island country.

As Waltz was detailing years of alleged corruption by the socialist government, members of the Cuban delegation, including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, began to slam on their designated table and yell for a point of order.
Then, as UN officials sought to tone down the outbursts, Rodríguez Parrilla walked down the aisle to the head of the General Assembly and yelled at Waltz, "You are a liar!"
Waltz responded, "You understand who you're dealing with? This is America. Back up."
Shouting erupts at UN embargo vote as U.S., Cuban officials face off

While the moment represented a shocking break from diplomatic decorum traditional to the UN, it perfectly captured the heightened tensions between Cuba and the U.S. as President Donald Trump's administration seeks to force changes to Cuba's political system by increasing its already punishing economic campaign.

The Caribbean country — already facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles — is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that affect basic activities such as cooking, the water supply and internet and telephone services.

Cuban officials have also repeatedly stressed that as U.S. officials demand that Cuba open up to private investment, Washington keeps piling on sanctions that stymie the very economic opening it has sought for decades.
A woman walks past a pool of sewage on a Havana street as water and electricity shortages threaten health and hygiene in the island nation. (Ricardo Arduengo/Reuters)

The outbursts Tuesday came a week after a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behaviour of the island's government.

Waltz and other U.S. officials have been using these public events and gatherings at the world body to try to persuade UN member states to vote on Wednesday against the annual resolution, which is aimed at calling out the U.S. government's "maximum pressure policy" against Cuba.

items: Canada faces challenge as it navigates growing calls to help Cuba amid U.S. aggression

blocks.text: For the past 34 years, the resolution has received overwhelming support. Last year, the vote was 165-7, with 12 abstentions. Argentina, Ukraine and Hungary opposed the measure for the first time.

Canada has consistently voted in favour of the annual resolution. Earlier this year, Global Affairs Canada announced it was providing $5.5 million in new support to Cubans, following $8 million it provided in February in accelerated funds to help scale up food aid to the nation.
While such resolutions are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Alexander brothers each sentenced to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking case
articles.summary: The three brothers were found guilty of drugging and raping several women over the course of decades.

blocks.text: Three brothers - two of them wealthy real-estate moguls - were sentenced to 30 years each in prison for drugging and raping dozens of women over the course of decades.

Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, were found guilty in March of using their wealth and social status to lure women to parties and luxury homes, where they sexually assaulted them.

On Tuesday morning, the court in New York heard from 12 victims, including one who did not testify during the trial, about the psychological trauma they endured after the Alexander brothers raped them and their desire for the shame they had felt to instead fall on the defendants.
Many asked the judge to impose the maximum sentence of life in prison for each brother.
Maya Miller told the court that after Tal Alexander raped her in 2014, she lost all sense of safety.
"I carry a quiet funeral within me for the person I might've become if this never happened to me," she said.
Another victim, who went by the pseudoym Isa Brooks, said after being raped by Tal and Alon Alexander when she was 16 years old, she lost the ability to trust herself.
"I had no idea the danger I was in til it was too late," she said.
Another woman said that when she planned to come forward about being raped, Tal Alexander threatened that he knew where her sister worked.

During the women's speeches, the three Alexander brothers showed little emotion. They stared ahead or conferred with their lawyers, who said they had advised their clients not to look at the victims while they spoke so it wasn't misconstrued as staring.
Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said the brothers deserved the maximum punishment for their crimes, saying the facts of the case "paint a truly devastating picture".
"For years, they honed their methods of luring women with the promise of luxury," she said, adding that they were "completely unmoved by the path of suffering they left behind them."

During the five-week trial, 11 women - including several who said they were minors at the time of the assaults - testified that the brothers gave them gifts and flew them to locations including Aspen and the Bahamas where they fed them drugs before raping them.
Prosecutors said the brothers' pattern of abusive behaviour began in high school, though the trial covered their crimes starting in 2008.

They had accused the three of slipping drugs in women's drinks, and said they "physically restrained and held down their victims during the rapes and sexual assaults and ignored screams and explicit requests to stop".
Lawyers for the brothers had argued the sex was consensual and that they were womanizers, but not sexual abusers. They pushedd for the lowest possible sentence for the brothers, 15 years.
Two of the brothers, Tal and Oren, made their wealth from selling luxury properties in New York and Miami.

They worked for American real estate giant Douglas Elliman, selling properties for celebrities including Lindsay Lohan, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West. In 2022, they founded their own New York-based firm called Official. Alon worked at the family's private security firm, Kent Security.
As they heard their sentences, the brotehrs did not react or show emotion, staring straight ahead.

articles.title: Former Met officer who served in same unit as David Carrick and Wayne Couzens found guilty of sexual offences
articles.summary:
Mark Tyrrell convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice at Southwark crown court

A former Metropolitan police officer who served in…

blocks.text: A former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same unit as Sarah Everard’s killer Wayne Couzens has been found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer.
A court heard that Mark Tyrrell raped the woman – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.
The 57-year-old was then said to have told her “I don’t believe what’s just happened” and “do you realise that what I’ve just done, that was rape?”
Tyrrell had been attached to the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, which is where the convicted rapists Couzens and David Carrick both worked.
He was convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice after a trial at Southwark crown court.
Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC alleged that when the woman resisted Tyrrell’s sexual advances “he simply chose to take what he wanted”.
The court heard that concerns were raised after officers attended her address for a separate matter and found Tyrrell hiding by the side of her bed.
The former PC was found guilty of perverting the course of justice by attempting to delete messages with the woman.
In one message, the court was told he said he was “sorry” for “being a sex offender” and “for ruining your life by being in it”.
Jurors found him not guilty in relation to 13 other charges, including one count of rape.
In his evidence, Tyrrell claimed sexual intercourse between them was always consensual and “there was never any forcefulness to it”.

Ch Supt Sara Leach, commander within specialist operations, said: “This kind of conduct is abhorrent but even more so when it is carried out by a serving officer, who had gained the trust of the victim.
“We remain appalled that someone like this was serving within our organisation and it is right he has been brought to justice.”
Tyrrell previously admitted misconduct in a public office. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to the police about why he was in her bedroom.
The defendant, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced on 16 December.
Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by then-Met officer Couzens in 2021. He was later given a whole-life order.
Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.

articles.title: Olivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressives
articles.summary:
Tightly fought election saw record turnout as incumbent mayor ran against her rival Brad Bradford

The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and…

blocks.text: The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressives councillors.

The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13 percentage point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared to Bradford’s 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city.

Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. Her win also signals voters see that progressive urban politics can resist cost-of-living backlash that has toppled over governments.
On Monday night, Chow thanked her supporters and Bradford.

“I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.”

Chow, 69, has long been a fixture of the city’s politics. She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what she received in 2023.

Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed.
While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years.
Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending.

In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate. For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers other vulnerable institutions.

In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.”
Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost.

Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. While Ford did not endorse her in this election, he told reporters the pair had a “phenomenal relationship” and said people should “read between the lines” when it comes to his preferred candidate. However, the two are likely to spar in a fierce battle over the city’s bike lanes.

Like other major urban centers, Toronto remains locked in a battle over affordability, an issue that is expected to remain a challenge for the incoming council, where a large number of progressive candidates both returned and won for the first time, including Diana McNally Chan, a well-known advocate for unhoused people, who will be the first renter to sit on city council.

articles.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
articles.summary: The truce was originally planned for the stranded residents of Oleshky, and Russia and Ukraine say no breaches have been reported.
articles.byline: Paul Kirby, Olga Malchevska, Dan Johnson

blocks.text: A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.

Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".

A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.

Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.

One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.

Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".

The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.

Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".

Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.

Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.

One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.

Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.
"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv.

blocks.text: Shoebridge to pitch increased welfare spending, hike in tax-free threshold

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, will address the National Press Club in Canberra today, promising to help Australians struggling with cost-of-living and answering questions about allegations against senator Jordon Steele-John.

He will propose lifting the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000, meaning people earning a wage won’t pay tax on their first $26,000. He says that will save the average working Australian more than $1,000.
The Greens are also proposing a $1,000 annual boost for people on income support, including pensioners, carers, students, and job seekers.
double quotation markNo matter who you are, whether you’re working, studying, looking for work or on a pension, you’ll get more than $1,000.

Costings for the Greens from the Parliamentary Budget Office show the plan would cost about $22bn a year, with Shoebridge proposing to pay for it through higher taxes on gas exports and a market-based tax on resources companies.
Steele-John is on leave from parliament amid an investigation into allegations about his conduct towards women. He has denied the allegations.

blocks.text: Australia pays biggest bill for global diesel crisis
Australia has paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, with a report putting the toll at $9bn over six months.
The added cost equates to $324 for every Australian, exceeding the bills incurred by Brazil, South Africa, France and the UK.
The Climate Council released the figures from its energy security scorecard on Wednesday, which also found Australia paid an extra $1.6bn for petrol imports.
The findings come days after oil prices reached a six-month high amid escalating threats in the Middle East.
- Australian Associated Press

blocks.caption: Australia has paid more than any other nation in additional fuel import costs since the Iran war. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters

blocks.text: No new numbers on social media ban deactivations due to investigations

The eSafety commissioner won’t release updated figures on the number of accounts held by under-16s that have been deactivated or suspended in compliance with the social media ban as investigations are underway into compliance with five of the platforms.

In March, the commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, announced that TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat were under investigation for compliance with the ban, and with new powers to compel the companies to produce documents, that investigation is under way, Inman Grant told Senate estimates last night.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has said more than 5m accounts have been deactivated across the 10 platforms required to comply, but no more updated figures will be coming while the investigations are ongoing as it may prejudice the outcome of those investigations, officials told Senate estimates.
No decision has been made as to whether to take any of the platforms to court to seek fines of nearly $100m for breaches of the law.
The government has resisted providing a public breakdown of the accounts deactivated across the 10 platforms but some companies – such as Meta and Snapchat – have provided their own figures.

Liberal senator Sarah Henderson requested the eSafety commissioner release the data publicly as “the numbers don’t add up”, indicating that the committee was provided much more detail privately by eSafety on the figures that had not been made public.
The question was taken on notice.

eSafety commissioner and family subjected to ‘onslaught of online abuse and threats’

blocks.caption: Josh Taylor

blocks.text: Josh Taylor
Australia’s eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, said she and her family had been subjected to an onslaught of online abuse and threats in the 10 years she has been in the role.

In her final appearance before Senate estimates last night, Inman Grant said it was a “sensitive and pivotal moment” for the parliament in the wake of the alleged attack on Helen Haines, and the environment was “dangerously febrile for women in senior government roles.”

double quotation markWhen public officials are used for political point scoring, a target goes on our backs and we are subjected to an onslaught of online abuse and threats. As many of you know, this has been the normal state of affairs for me and my family for years, yet somehow this is meant to be accepted as part of public service.

blocks.caption: e-Safety commissioner Julie Inman Grant. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

blocks.text: Inman Grant did not name any people who have targeted her personally, but her work in the role has seen her labelled as a “censorship commissar” by the world’s richest person, Elon Musk. US Republican congressman Jim Jordan labelled Inman Grant as a “zealot for global takedowns”.
Inman Grant said more needs to be done for the next generation of leaders to feel safe in online spaces or public-facing roles.

double quotation markSocial media is no longer the once envisioned digital town square – it has become more like a gladiatorial arena. Meanwhile, platforms continue to roll back abuse and violent speech policies that let some of the most egregious offenders out of digital jail.

Inflation expected to rise to 4.2%

blocks.caption: Patrick Commins

blocks.text: Patrick Commins

Official data released at 11:30am are expected to show inflation accelerated to 4.2% in the year to September, from 4% in the month before, as rising fuel costs amid a worsening Middle East conflict compound cost of living pressures.

Look out for the Reserve Bank’s preferred gauge of underlying inflation, which removes the most volatile prices. That measure is predicted to hold at 3.6% in the year to the September quarter, economists say, but anything higher will virtually guarantee a fifth interest rate hike next Tuesday.

The RBA may feel the need to hike regardless, as recent comments from top central bank officials suggest they are more worried about high inflation becoming entrenched in the system than the rising rate of unemployment.
Financial markets are pricing in about a 65% chance of a Melbourne Cup day rate rise.
The latest inflation report also lands in the middle of a parliamentary sitting week, and the opposition will be quick to use the figures to attack Labor for its management of the economy.

Rising unemployment and accelerating inflation is not a situation anyone is comfortable with. But a more benign set of numbers today will take the heat off mortgaged households, the Reserve Bank and the Albanese government.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Kat Wong with the main action.

Australia’s eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, told Senate estimates last night that she and her family had been subjected to an onslaught of online abuse and threats in the 10 years she has been in the role. More details in a minute.

The latest inflation figures will be released at 11.30am and are expected to show an increase in prices of 4.2% in the year to September. That means the chances of a rate hike on Melbourne Cup day next week will also rise. More coming up.

articles.title: Unpaid carers say chancellor’s plan to scrap allowance cliff edge falls short
articles.summary:
Digital taper system for benefit expected in budget, but those already hit with overpayments will still have to pay

“On the surface it sounds really positive – and I really hope that it is,”…

blocks.text: “On the surface it sounds really positive – and I really hope that it is,” says unpaid carer Guy Shahar of the government’s decision to abolish the notorious carer’s allowance cliff edge.

But Shahar is angry that most carers hit with unjust overpayments in the past will still have to repay them, for all the promise of a different future. And he notes that the cliff edge remains in place for four more years, potentially catching out more carers.
“They are effectively saying: ‘We know that the system was unfair but we will still punish you for having been the victim of an unfair system,’” he says.

The chancellor is expected to announce the introduction of a new digital taper system into the carer’s allowance benefit in the budget, in effect ending a rule that has landed hundreds of thousands of carers with life-shattering financial penalties.

Unpaid carers have broadly welcomed the move – and there is a general acknowledgment that ministers are moving positively, if slowly, to reform a system with inbuilt injustices and terrible management that birthed what became known as the carer’s allowance scandal.

But there is also disbelief that the new system – which must be built from scratch – will be live before 2030, and a feeling that the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has a lot more to do to regain the trust of unpaid carers.

blocks.caption: Elizabeth Tait, who looks after her disabled son, Oliver, says the cliff edge symbolises a ‘whole crazy system’. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: Shahar and his wife, Oksana, who care for their autistic son, Daniel, were victims of the cliff edge. This rule meant that a carer who earns more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – will forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, now £86.45.

A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40. Last year, the Shahars were landed with a £10,000 repayment bill for relatively trivial earnings breaches dating back five years.

Oksana had earned more than the allowed limit by just £1.92 a week on average while juggling caring with part-time minimum wage jobs. In some weeks, she was paid just 38p more than the carer’s allowance earnings threshold.

Over the period, she earned a total of £505 more than the rules allowed – but was duly issued with a bill for £10,130.45 – plus a £50 civil penalty. The Shahars are challenging the charge at tribunal but the stress is real and ongoing.

Unpaid carer Elizabeth Tait, who looks after her disabled son, Oliver, is staggered that the taper system is years away: “We live in the age of tech; it is ludicrous it is going to take so long. They need to make it a priority.”

Tait, a former teacher and now a private tutor and educational consultant who ended up with a bill for £1,623 after unwittingly breaching the earnings threshold, says the carer’s allowance cliff edge symbolises a “whole crazy system”.

Reforming carer’s allowance is essential but it needs to be part of a wider examination of the crucial role of unpaid care in propping up England’s social care arrangements, she says: “We care willingly and lovingly, and yet we end up a casualty of the system.”

Andrea Tucker, who for years acted as an unpaid carer for her mother, is one of a handful of carers to challenge a cliff edge penalty and win, successfully overturning a £4,600 overpayment at a tribunal in February 2025.

blocks.caption: Andrea Tucker, who for years acted as an unpaid carer for her mother, challenged the cliff edge penalty and won but says it cost her months of stress. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian

blocks.text: As a result, she did not have to repay the money, although she suffered months of stress along the way. She welcomes the decision to introduce a taper but believes carers punished unfairly by draconian rules should be compensated.
“People repaying overpayments should no longer have to, and they should be given back what they have already paid,” she says.

Tucker recalls how for years she carefully monitored her monthly earnings from her part-time charity shop role to stay under the limit. Some weeks she would work six hours for nothing so as not to risk losing carer’s allowance.
Even so, she was hit with an overpayment when DWP officials decided – unlawfully – that she could not average her earnings over a one-year period.

There is raw bitterness among carers about the cliff edge, she says. “My friend is paying back their overpayment at £10 a month. She went £12.50 over as a result of receiving holiday pay. She always tells me: ‘I hope I die before I have paid it all back.’”

articles.title: Legacy of 7 October looms large as a divided Israel goes to the polls in record numbers
articles.summary:
Bereaved families tell voters to remember the victims while others have flown thousands of miles to cast their ballots

Election day in Israel began with a protest by some of the voters with…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison in Efrat and Julian Borger in Nazareth

blocks.text: Election day in Israel began with a protest by some of the voters with most at stake. Bereaved families of those killed in the 7 October attacks held a minute of silence at 6.29am, the moment when Hamas launched its onslaught just over three years ago.

They gathered in a Tel Aviv plaza that has become known as “hostages square” because it was the centre of demonstrations demanding the return of more than 200 captives from Gaza. Holding pictures of their loved ones, they stood in silence then called on voters to remember the losses and betrayals of that day when deciding on the next government.
“Three years after the massacre, our loved ones will not be voting today. Go out and vote – remember them at the ballot box. This is what these elections are about,” the group said.

They are not explicitly backing any political party, but one of their key demands is a state commission of inquiry into the attacks. Benjamin Netanyahu has resisted this and it has become a rallying point for the opposition parties trying to unseat him as prime minister.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, casts his vote in Herzliya. He said Benjamin Netanyahu had led the worst government Israel had known. Photograph: Shir Torem/Reuters

blocks.text: Netanyahu’s strongest challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, started the day by visiting communities attacked on 7 October. “If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here,” said the former military chief and leader of the Yashar party.

Standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”. He noted that victory wasn’t certain, adding that “we are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state”.
As the day wore on, it became clear that voter turnout was shattering all records and among those lining up at polling stations were tens of thousands of Israelis who live overseas.

blocks.caption: A polling station in the Jewish settlement of Efrat in the West Bank. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: A bipartisan “Fly&Vote” initiative was set up to support those who wanted to return because electoral law only allows voting in person. While not everyone coming back was opposed to the government, anecdotal evidence suggested many were opposition supporters who held the view that Israel faced an existential choice.

Monica Moria, 58, and her husband, Ron, flew in to Tel Aviv from Barcelona. They took a train to a kibbutz where she is registered to vote and she cast her ballot for the most leftwing of the Jewish Israeli parties, the Democrats.

She said: “It feels like Israel has lost its way, there are deep divisions and hatreds that will be very difficult to heal. The idea is to bring a political change so that we can bring Israeli society together again. I want to be optimistic, but I am also afraid.”
Kobi Mizrahi, 35, who has been completing a PhD in New York, paid more than $1,600 (£1,200) to come back to Israel for just a few days and vote.

He said: “Given the fact that it feels like a ‘now or never’ moment, where if we lose these elections to the Bibi coalition this might be the turning point we can’t come back to, I felt like I have to do anything in my power to help.”

blocks.caption: Yuval Schwarzfuchs, right, flew all the way from Rio de Janeiro to vote for the Joint List in Jerusalem.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Yuval Schwarzfuchs, 26, travelled from Rio de Janeiro via Ethiopia to vote for the Palestinian-led Joint List. “For me, its about equality for all,” he said. “I did what I had to do.”
He came to the Jerusalem polling station wearing a T-shirt with an image of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the leftwing president of Brazil, who defied the polls to win re-election at the weekend.
In the settlement of Efrat near Jerusalem, Shani, 19, had come to the polling station with her parents, to cast her vote for the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich.
She is part of a large cohort of first-time voters who are more rightwing than older generations and may help bolster support for Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners.

More than 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the last election in 2022, and three-quarters of first-time Jewish voters define themselves as right or centre-right, a poll for Channel 12 television found (it did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel).

Shani said she chose Smotrich, a settler himself, for his promises to expand Israel’s footprint in occupied Palestine. “Smotrich is pushing forward with settlement expansion and improving security,” she said.
Her mother, kindergarten teacher Rivka, also voted for Smotrich, and said her priority was to return Netanyahu’s coalition to office.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian family walks past election campaign posters in Beit Kahil in the West Bank on Tuesday. Palestinian parties in Israel may hold the balance of power in what is expected to be a tight result. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The right must win, because otherwise there is a chance of a Palestinian state, which will be very bad for Jews,” she said.

Spiralling attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinians, and the growing threat of sanctions on settlement goods and construction, were not a key election issue for voters in Efrat who spoke to the Guardian.

The Palestinian Israeli vote is a critical camp in this election, representing about a fifth of eligible voters. Their votes are expected to go to either Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, or Joint List, an electoral alliance of Palestinian-Israeli parties.

Even if the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot wins more seats than Netanyahu’s coalition, it is not expected to win an outright majority. It has also ruled out going into coalition with the Palestinian Israeli parties, which could well hold the balance of power.
Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the leading party in the Joint List coalition, thinks Eisenkot’s approach may change after the elections.
“He cannot sit down [in coalition] with Netanyahu, and he won’t want to go back to another round of elections, so we think he can be flexible,” he said.

blocks.caption: Arab voters who are Israeli citizens cast their ballots at a polling station in Nazareth, Israel. Turnout was high in the city. Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Nazareth, the largest Palestinian-majority town in Israel, the turnout at polling stations has been noticeably higher than at recent elections, although still below the average Jewish turnout across the country. A surge of evening voting was expected here as people came home from work.
At the headquarters of the Joint List, the most pressing concern was the spoiler tactics of far-right election monitors at predominantly Palestinian polling stations.

“They can say that they want to check all the voter numbers and identity and everything, so they can slow things down, so that people wait a long time and give up. That’s their intention,” said Shbita.
At worst, these ploys have slowed the process down so that it took half an hour to vote, rather than a couple of minutes, he added.
Shbita said voters were sufficiently motivated to overcome such obstacles. “It is the first time for a long time that a government has stayed in office for its full term, four years,” he said.

“We are talking about one of the worst governments when it comes to Arab society. We feel racism at all levels of Israeli society, in hospitals, in buses, in public transportation, in the media. So people understand that today we have the opportunity to change the government.”

articles.title: Serial Calgary rapist from 1980s convicted of 9 offences against mothers, teen girl
articles.summary: A serial rapist who targeted vulnerable victims who were home alone with young children at the time they were attacked has been convicted of his crimes more than 40 years after the fact.

image.caption: Richard Hubert Jones has been found guilty of nine offences relating to three rapes he committed in the 1980s. (David Mercer/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A serial rapist who targeted vulnerable victims who were home alone with young children at the time they were attacked has been convicted of his crimes more than 40 years after the fact.
Richard Hubert Jones, 72, will be sentenced at later date
A serial rapist who targeted vulnerable victims in Calgary who were home alone with young children at the time they were attacked has been convicted of his crimes more than 40 years after the fact.
Richard Hubert Jones, 72, was found guilty of nine offences stemming from the rapes of a 13-year-old girl and two single mothers in 1984 and 1985.
Calgary police investigated, but the case went cold.

Jones got away with his crimes for more than four decades until advances in investigation techniques led Calgary Police Service detectives from cold case and sexual assault units to track down Jones via family members who’d submitted DNA to genealogy databases.

items: Judge hears accounts of Calgary women, teen terrorized by serial rapist in 1980s as case nears conclusion

blocks.text: In May 2023, Jones was arrested and charged after those investigators matched his DNA to samples collected from the victims, their clothing and the crime scenes.
One of Jones’ victims died before she could see her rapist charged and convicted.
Defence did not argue against conviction

Last month, a hearing took place during which Jones admitted that his DNA was a match to the samples collected by police in the 1980s and signed an agreed statement of facts that detailed the crimes against each victim.
Defence lawyers Julie Grivel and Lance McClean called no evidence and did not argue against a conviction.
On Tuesday, Justice Christopher Simard ruled the Crown had proven all of the elements of each offence, including the identity of the rapist.
“I find the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Jones is guilty of all the charged offences,” said Simard. “I convicted you.”
Jones to remain on bail
The way in which the case proceeded — in contrast with a guilty plea — protects Jones’ path to appeal the pre-trial decisions relating to admissible evidence.
But first, Jones will be sentenced for his crimes. A date for that hearing will be set later this week. In the meantime, he remains on bail.
The Crown indicated there will be victim impact statements filed as part of the sentencing process. A publication ban protects their identities. CBC News will use their initials.
The details of what happened to each victim come from the agreed statement of facts.
13-year-old victim
On Feb. 20, 1984, T.N., then 13, was babysitting her little brother when Jones broke into her Thorncliffe house.
Jones took the eight-year-old boy by the hand and led him to a bedroom, returned and removed T.N.’s nightgown and proceeded to rape her.
When he was finished, he left, threatening to return and kill her if she told anyone.
T.N. grabbed her brother and ran to a neighbour’s home for help.
Mother attacked while child slept
A month later, Jones struck again. This time, he broke into the home of C.T., a 30-year-old single mother who’d fallen asleep beside her nine-year-old son while reading him bedtime stories.
C.T. woke up to Jones standing at the foot of her bed. She told police she ran to get him away from her son.
Jones attacked, first in the living room, and then led her by her neck to her son’s bedroom, where he raped her.
After he finished, he threatened to return if she tried to identify him.
Daughter found mom 'in shambles'
The third attack took place more than a year later in the city’s southwest.
N.C., a 33-year-old single mother fell asleep on her sofa in June 1985 and woke up to a man’s hand over her mouth.
It was Jones.
He told her he’d been watching her for three days. He held her by her hair, pushed her to the stairs, removed her clothing and raped her.
N.C.’s 12-year-old daughter woke up and came to the top of the stairs. Her mother yelled at her to stay where she was.
After Jones left, the child came downstairs to find her mother “in shambles.” They called police.
N.C. died in 2007.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Dutch zookeeper dies after being mauled in leopard enclosure
articles.summary: The woman began her career at the park when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.

blocks.text: An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.
The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.
She sustained injuries to her head and neck but despite undergoing surgery, the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.
An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.
Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.

"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.
The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.

Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injures she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition before she died days later.
A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.
"They are, and remain, predators."
Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

articles.title: RAF Fairford plot ‘coordinated by handler working on behalf of Iran’
articles.summary:
Two men charged under National Security Act were directed by handler believed to have been working for Iranian intelligence, court told

A group of men were directed to drive vans loaded with…

blocks.text: A group of men were directed to drive vans loaded with petrol to Fairford RAF base by a handler known as Ali, who police believe was working on behalf of Iran, a court heard on Tuesday.

One of the five men tasked with driving to the base called police in the early hours of 27 September after the handler warned the group about a bomb in the vans, prosecutors told Westminster magistrates court.
Two men, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both appeared in court on Tuesday charged under the National Security Act 2023.
Abdulkarim, of London, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service. He is accused of buying the vans used in the Fairford incident on the instruction of Ali.

Essghir, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, after initially being arrested at the scene near the Gloucestershire base on 27 September and then re-arrested on 20 October. He is accused of visiting RAF Fairford and filming around the facility on a video call with Ali before returning a month later in the convoy of vans.
Abdulkarim has been released on bail under conditions including the surrender of his passport, and Essghir has been remanded in custody. They will appear at the Old Bailey on 20 November.
Prosecutor Louise Gray alleged the defendants were in contact with an individual known as Ali who is now believed to be abroad.
She said that during the events of 27 September at the RAF Fairford base, five men who were arrested travelled in vans, parked and got out “and were told to do so by someone known as Mr Ali”.
One of them, she said, had claimed they were told there was a bomb in the van and called 999.

The court heard that the person calling stated that they were from London and that he was one of a group of five males. The caller told the police that they had been tasked to drive vans to the location for the purpose of a new business venture. When the vans arrived at the location, the organiser was in communication with them over the telephone.

Gray alleged he then told them to park the vans and to walk away from them. After they did that, the organiser told them to run as he had planted a bomb in the van. The caller indicated that he and his colleagues had run away from the vans and were now calling the police for help.
The defendants are believed to have known Ali for “a number of years”, she said.
Essghir is accused of travelling to RAF Fairford on 22 August and contacting Ali.
Abdulkarim is accused of buying mobile phones and collecting cash for Ali, as well as buying five vans including the three that were driven to RAF Fairford.
The court heard he had known Ali for 10 years and it was claimed the latter had been linked to a drone incident at the Israeli embassy.
Counter Terror Policing said they believed the foreign intelligence service involved in the case was Iranian.

The assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of national counter-terrorism policing in the UK, said: “We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the director general of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat.
“The public can help us with this, and as always I would urge them to report anything that they’re worried about – those reports can and do make a difference.”

A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national who was also arrested on 20 October on suspicion of aiding Iran’s intelligence service has been released without charge but remains on police bail after being arrested on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.
Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail.

Frank Ferguson, the chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute two individuals with National Security Act offences following a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford. We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues.”

articles.title: Ottawa Rapid FC pull merch naming nonexistent 'Van Blurené Parc'
articles.summary: Ever heard of Ottawa's Van Blurené Parc or gazed upon the giant sign on the national gallery? That alternate version of Ottawa was briefly on merchandise for the Ottawa Rapid soccer team before it…

blocks.text: Ottawa·New

Ever heard of Ottawa's Van Blurené Parc or gazed upon the giant sign on the national gallery? That alternate version of Ottawa was briefly on merchandise for the Ottawa Rapid soccer team before it was pulled.
Text changed by production partner, club says
Some Ottawa Rapid merchandise has been removed from its website after CBC Ottawa made inquiries about errors in the design. (Ottawa Rapid FC)
Ever heard of Ottawa's Van Blurené Parc or gazed upon the giant sign on the national gallery?
That alternate version of Ottawa was briefly on merchandise for the Ottawa Rapid soccer team before it was pulled.

Earlier this month, a fan of the Northern Super League club reached out to CBC Ottawa to flag problems with an $85 sweater she'd seen in the team's store, questioning whether it was made using artificial intelligence (AI).
The design on the sweater and other merchandise features illustrations of Ottawa landmarks with short phrases like "Bytown" and "Rideau Falls" interspersed throughout.
But it also featured several questionable elements, which CBC asked the soccer team about:

items: A reference to "Van Blurené Parc," which is not a park in the city.
An architecturally inaccurate depiction of the National Gallery of Canada.
An illustration of the spider sculpture Maman, which sits outside the gallery, that's missing a leg.
A missing apostrophe from the phrase "Canada's Capital."

blocks.text: Some of the detail on a shirt for sale. (Ottawa Rapid FC)
In response, Ottawa Rapid said that Marcus Farias, the Toronto-based artist behind the design, told them no generative AI was used on his end.
CBC News reached out to Farias directly, but did not hear back by deadline.
The club said the drawings were not intended as an architecturally or geographically precise representation of the city.

"The original artwork was intentionally a stylized interpretation of Ottawa, with creative licence taken in depicting the city's landmarks," according to a statement from Shawna Newbery, the club's chief marketing officer.

As for the textual errors, the club said the text had been changed by its production partner from what the artist had originally created. They did not confirm how or why that was done before deadline.
The team did say the reference to "Van Blurené Parc" originally read "Viam Prepare Parati," which seems to be a mix of Latin and English.
The Rapid said Marcus Farias, a Toronto-based artist, confirmed that no generative AI was used to create this original art in question. (Marcus Farias)

"The changes to the lettering on the finished merchandise, including the reference to a non-existent park, did not reflect the intended design and should have been identified before the products went on sale," wrote Newbery.
She said the club is working with its partners to understand how the issues occurred and establish a stronger review and approval process, and may produce a revised version of the original design.
The club has withdrawn all merchandise featuring the affected design, it said, and will offer "full refunds to supporters who wish to return their purchases."
"We take pride in representing Ottawa, and our supporters deserve that same care and attention to detail in everything we do," Newbery wrote.

articles.title: Trump wades into Canadian politics with kudos for Parti Québécois, B.C. Conservative wins
articles.summary: While he is fully engaged in a tight midterm election battle in his own country, U.S. President Donald Trump is still finding time to step into politics north of the border by congratulating the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump congratulated the new premiers of Quebec and B.C. in a pair of social media posts on Tuesday — a highly unusual move for a foreign leader. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

While he is fully engaged in a tight midterm election battle in his own country, U.S. President Donald Trump is still finding time to step into politics north of the border by congratulating the recently elected premiers of Quebec and British Columbia.
Comments come as Trump administration accuses Canada of U.S. election interference

While he's fully engaged in a tight midterm election battle in his own country, U.S. President Donald Trump is still finding time to step into politics north of the border by congratulating the newly elected premiers of Quebec and British Columbia.
Praise for the sovereignist premier of Quebec, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, and Conservative premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, came Tuesday in a pair of posts on Trump's Truth Social platform.
The highly unusual move breaks with the tradition of U.S. presidents and Canadian prime ministers only offering public congratulations to their direct counterparts.

Trump's praise of St-Pierre Plamondon came with a dig at Prime Minister Mark Carney. He linked to an article in the Irish Times carrying the headline: "Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney."
Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet responded by suggesting Trump's comments would be more relevant if he wanted to talk about cutting tariffs.
"Actually Mr. Trump is unpredictable and not so meaningful of what he says.... There's no lost love between Quebecers and Mr. Trump," Blanchet said.
Trump congratulating new Quebec premier 'not so meaningful': Bloc leader
The salute to Doerkson's "big victory" was described by the president as an example of conservatives "moving strong in Canada."
Trump first congratulated the incoming B.C. premier on the night of his election win, in a post that was shared by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra on X.
The B.C. Conservatives' win on Saturday was the party's first victory in about a century, a fact noted in that post.
Conservative doesn't equal MAGA

Hoekstra's message was reposted by several prominent Conservatives who, rather than join in the celebration, criticized the president for his lack of knowledge about Canada and his ambassador's decision to amplify it.

"It is impressive how bad you are at understanding the basic elements of your job or the simple truths of the country you are privileged to live in," former Conservative cabinet minister James Moore wrote to Hoekstra.

Stephen Harper's former communications director, Dimitri Soudas, quoted Doerkson's comments from September about "unacceptable threats, tariffs and rhetoric from a bully south of the border" as he shared Hoekstra's post.

items: U.S. says Carney government brushing off 'potential interference'
Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown

blocks.text: Ken Boessenkool, a former senior policy adviser to Harper and the federal Conservative Party, tried to explain that being conservative in Canada doesn't mean being aligned with Trump.

"The MAGA party in B.C. is called One B.C. They got 1.5 per cent of the vote. More than Trump would get, I suspect," Boessenkool said in a post on X, referring to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.
"Like you, they are an embarrassment to the concept of conservatism."
Election interference and endorsements
Polls show Trump's dispute with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.

Many online drew attention to the irony of the Trump administration's accusations that Canada is interfering in the U.S. midterm elections — where polling suggests the Republicans are struggling — while poking his own nose into Canada's politics.
The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a "fact sheet" last week pointing to instances that could amount to "potential interference in U.S. elections" including the Nov. 3 midterms.
That accusation came despite Trump's record of endorsing political candidates around the world since returning to the White House.
Since early 2025, Trump has backed presidential or prime ministerial candidates in Poland, Honduras, Colombia and Japan.
Most recently, he voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The U.S. president also put his support behind former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán's failed re-election bid, which included Vice-President JD Vance appearing at a rally in Budapest.

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.
