articles.title: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
articles.summary: Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the…

blocks.text: When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.

The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.

Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.

As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.

Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio speaking to the media in the Taj Mahal Palace hotel in Mumbai last Wednesday.  Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump the deal-maker

Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.

But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.

The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.

“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.

But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.

“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.

In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.

As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward

Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.

“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.

His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”

If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

blocks.text: Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:

“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”

blocks.text: That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Prarthna Singh captured the rkivecity menswear line through a female gaze.   Photograph: Prarthna Singh

blocks.text: Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.

“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

articles.title: N.S. woman refused to comply with phone scammer, so would-be fraudster swatted her house
articles.summary: A Truro-area woman says she is shaken and terrified after a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police from two different departments to her home over the weekend.

image.caption: Lynn Clark Colpitts says a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police officers from two different departments to her home over the weekend after she refused to go along with a scam. (Galen McRae/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
A Truro-area woman says she is shaken and terrified after a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police from two different departments to her home over the weekend.
'There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong,' says Lynn Clark Colpitts

The original call seemed like a routine phone scam. A woman claiming to be from the CIBC fraud department called Lynn Clark Colpitts and said someone had applied for a credit card in her name. In order to block it, she advised Clark Colpitts to download an app called CIBC Guard.

Colpitts said she didn’t feel comfortable doing that or sharing any information over the phone. While she was on the call she conferenced her IT expert from work into the call who told her to do nothing until she contacted her branch.
"I told her politely, I said I'm sorry I have to go by what my IT guy told me to do. And then she used some profanity toward me,” Clark Colpitts said.
“She called me a f-----g b---h, twice, and then hung up on me.”
Clark Colpitts figured she’d dodged a scam but 20 minutes later things escalated.
'She was threatening me the whole time'
“She calls me back and says, ‘I've got a surprise for you. Go to your front door. There's a surprise waiting for you there.’ And I'm like, ‘What are you talking about?’"
Sure enough, as she stepped onto her porch she saw heavily armed officers from the Colchester District RCMP and Truro Police in her yard and on the street.
“They holler at me and ask me who I am,” Clark Colpitts said. “And I tell them who I am and they tell me to get down to the end of the driveway.”

Several officers entered her home while Clark Colpitts tried to explain there was no such threat. While police checked on the property the fraudster kept up the phone calls to Clark Colpitts. She held it up so police could hear it.
“She was threatening me the whole time saying that she wasn't done with me and that this was gonna keep going on.”
RCMP explained to Clark Colpitts that they’d gotten a call about a hostage taking — and shooting — at her address.
Calls, emails and death threats
“It appears to be a level of retribution by the fraudsters in this case,” said Staff Sgt. Mark Rose, commander of the Colchester District RCMP.
“[It appears] they did this to cause her harm and pain and distress by having the police respond to her residence all because she didn’t follow the original instructions on the phone."
The calls from the female fraudster continued on Friday and into Saturday.
Staff Sgt. Mark Rose is the commander of the Colchester District RCMP. (Galen McRae/CBC)
“She just kept going on and on and on. It was relentless," Clark Colpitts said.
And there were emails too. Death threats.

Clark Colpitts is a realtor. She got a phone call from a coworker who said someone had hacked into their agency’s website, took down Clark Colpitts's photograph and replaced it with what Clark Colpitts says was a “deformed animal.” All of it has left her scared to be in her own home.
Swatting attack

David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security, which is based in Fredericton, says Canadians have lost tens of millions of dollars to phone scams, but this is the first time he’s aware of it escalating into a “swatting” attack. That’s when a person calls police to someone’s property to report a crime or emergency that is entirely fiction.
“This seems like a criminal who was definitely not having a good day and decided to dramatically escalate the dangerousness and seriousness of this situation,” Shipley said.

“I would argue that this is a form of terrorism,” he said. “Canadians aren't used to having the SWAT team from the police department show up with assault rifles and body armour and riot shields to their front door. That's incredibly, incredibly traumatic.”

items: More stories from Northern Nova Scotia

blocks.text: Rose said police have to take these calls at face value and deliver the appropriate response.

“We've offered victim support services to [Clark Colpitts] and we are working with our law enforcement partners in other countries — and in Canada — to determine if this connects to other offences and try to determine who's responsible for this.”

CIBC told CBC News in a statement that there is no app called "CIBC Guard" and that it would never contact customers requesting personal or financial information, or request you download an app. It urged people to be extremely cautious when dealing with unsolicited emails, texts or phone calls, and not to rely on caller ID.
The bank said it's actively working to educate clients about impersonation and other scams, and it urges people to contact 911 if there is an urgent threat to their safety or the safety of others.
Meanwhile Clark Colpitts says she's traumatized.
“There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong.”

articles.title: Solidum says no need to hoard water as supply sufficient amid El Niño
articles.summary: There is no need to hoard water amid the El Niño phenomenon as supply remains sufficient in the next several months, Department of Science and Technology Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 4:53pm

ANGELES, Pampanga —There is no need to hoard water amid the El Niño phenomenon as supply remains sufficient in the next several months, Department of Science and Technology Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said.
"Dapat nga hindi nagho-hoard [ng tubig] because wala namang issue pa," Solidum said during a press conference in Angeles, Pampanga.
(People should not hoard water because there's no issue yet.)
He added that the public should not worry, especially in areas with well-managed dams and water conservation measures.
Solidum, instead, urged the public to save rainwater and use for household needs like washing the car and watering the plants.
"Bakit ka pa mag-i-imbak ng drinking water kung may supply pa naman? Kasi priority ng government niyan to supply the drinking water," Solidum said.
(Why store drinking water when there’s still a supply available? The government’s priority is to ensure the supply of drinking water.)
"But in case lang na may mga lugar na talagang walang-wala, then that's the time you actually use it (stored water)," he added.
(But only in cases where certain areas are completely without water should you actually use the water you’ve stored.)
As of 8 a.m., Angat Dam’s water level slightly decreased to 209.19 meters from 209.33 meters recorded on Sunday.
The dam's minimum operating level is 180 meters, while its normal high water level is at 210 meters.
Angat Dam supplies around 90% of the water needs of Metro Manila, Rizal, and portions of Cavite and Bulacan.

articles.title: Woman files abuse complaint vs live-in partner cop
articles.summary: A woman from Mindanao on Tuesday filed an administrative complaint against her live-in partner, a police officer, over alleged abuse for nearly nine years, the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM)…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 4:52pm

A woman from Mindanao on Tuesday filed an administrative complaint against her live-in partner, a police officer, over alleged abuse for nearly nine years, the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) said.
In a statement, the NAPOLCOM said the complainant, who is a teacher, filed the complaint against Police Corporal Ricardo Silva Jr., who is assigned at Camp Crame in Quezon City.

“Hindi natin papayagan ang anumang uri ng karahasan laban sa kababaihan. Sa mga nakararanas ng pang-aabuso, huwag po kayong pumayag na saktan kayo, kahit sa unang pagkakataon pa lamang,” NAPOLCOM Commissioner Ralph Calinisan said at a press conference.
(We will not tolerate any form of violence against women. To those who are experiencing abuse, do not allow yourself to be harmed, even for the first time.)
“Magsumbong po kayo sa awtoridad. Nandiyan ang PNP at ang NAPOLCOM para makinig, tumulong, at umalalay sa inyo,” he added.
(Report it to the authorities. The PNP and NAPOLCOM are here to listen, help, and support you.)
Calinisan vowed to pursue appropriate administrative proceedings against Silva for grave misconduct and conduct unbecoming of a police officer.
During the press briefing, the complainant, identified as alias “Ma’am” recounted how she sought help after feeling that she could no longer escape her abusive situation.

“Sa lahat ng battered women diyan, oras na po para lumabas kayo. Huwag n’yo na pong tiisin. Huwag niyo nang hintayin na masiraan kayo ng bait, mawala ang mga pangarap n’yo sa buhay, o mawala ang mga pinaghirapan ninyo. Huwag n’yo nang hintaying sirain kayo ng isang taong hindi naman karapat-dapat,” she said.

(To all the battered women out there, it's time to come out. Don't put up with it anymore. Don't wait for your sanity, dreams, or things you worked hard for to be destroyed. Don't wait for someone who doesn't deserve it to destroy you.)
For his part, Silva apologized for his actions and urged fellow police officers not to follow his example.

“Sorry, Hon, sa nagawa ko. Sa mga kabaro ko, huwag n’yo akong tularan. Kung masama man ang loob n’yo, magdasal na lang. Sa lahat ng tao, humihingi po ako ng paumanhin sa mali kong nagawa,” Silva said during the press conference.
(Sorry, Hon, for what I did. To my colleagues, don't imitate me. If you have bad feelings, just pray. To everyone, I apologize for the wrong I did.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Long-term medication or modern crash diet? Inside the new world of GLP-1s
articles.summary: GLP-1s were designed and tested for long-term use, to combat chronic health conditions like diabetes and obesity. But what happens when you take these blockbuster weight loss drugs for a short stint?…

image.caption: GLP-1s were designed and tested for long-term use to combat chronic health conditions like diabetes and obesity. But what happens when you take these blockbuster weight loss drugs for a short stint? Scientists are trying to find out. (Matthew Hoddy/CBC)

blocks.text: At a bridal shop in downtown Halifax, Beverley Smith is trying on wedding dresses, but there’s a catch: She's rapidly losing weight since starting a GLP-1.

The 32-year-old has already gone on and off several types of these popular medications to manage weight gain and other side-effects linked to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), but decided to get serious about her health before getting married next summer.
She’s lost more than 30 pounds since starting the drug tirzepatide back in March, and says related symptoms — like joint pain — have improved as well.
Now she’s asking the same question as millions of GLP-1 users around the world: Is it possible to one day stop taking the drug that’s changed life for the better?
"When you are going off it…. do you taper off of it or do you stop abruptly?" Smith wondered. "What is this really going to look like in the long term?"
As these blockbuster drugs explode in popularity, with more people using them off-label for short-term weight loss, scientists are also striving to find an answer.
"This is a real-world situation that needs to be studied," said Dr. Thomas Leung, a clinician-scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, who’s among the researchers doing exactly that.
Microdosing, drug cycling and more
GLP-1 drugs work by suppressing blood sugar, controlling appetite and slowing stomach emptying, all by mimicking their namesake hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, which is released after you eat.

items: 3 million Canadians use GLP-1 drugs. Survey says that's changing their appetites — and habits
Should everyone be on GLP-1s? What the science really tells us about cancer prevention and other benefits

blocks.text: While these medications only became part of the zeitgeist in the last few years — driven by celebrity endorsements, before hitting the mainstream — they’ve been around for more than two decades.

The earliest forms were studied and approved to treat Type 2 diabetes. Later, options arrived for chronic weight management. What’s relatively new is the myriad ways people are using these medications, often with minimal medical supervision.

At a private appointment inside Kind Bridal in Halifax, Beverley Smith tries on a wedding dress and discusses alterations to accommodate her ongoing weight loss while using a GLP-1. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)
Many patients — or as some drugmakers now call them, "customers" — are treating GLP-1s like a yo-yo diet rather than taking them long term to manage chronic health conditions.

They’re ever easier to get through online pharmacies. And pill forms, versus injections, are becoming more accessible. (Though not yet available in Canada, there is a pill-based form of semaglutide — the drug best known by the brand name Ozempic — already approved in the U.S. from drugmaker Novo Nordisk, alongside a pill version of orforglipron from Eli Lilly.)

items: 1st generic semaglutide injection for weight loss approved: Health Canada

blocks.text: Scroll through social media and it’s easy to find a range of short-term uses, from bodybuilders cycling through different types of GLP-1s (and steroids, too) alongside their gym routines to women "microdosing" the drugs off and on to manage menopausal weight gain to brides and grooms doing quick stints to lose weight before their wedding day.
One recent study from a Danish research team looked at the use of semaglutide for obesity and found roughly half of adults stopped treatment within just 12 months.
Ozempic, other GLP-1 drugs may help with dozens of other conditions
Stop-and-start approach could hinder weight loss

It’s a trend Dr. Leung, the researcher from the University of Pennsylvania, noticed in his own social circle in recent years, as more of his friends and colleagues wanted to try GLP-1s just to drop a few pounds.

Some talked about wanting to shed weight before a vacation or to look good on Instagram or just to feel healthier. The common thread? A desire to go on the meds, then get off them as fast as possible.

"No one had really studied what happens when you model what human behaviour is, which is starting and stopping these drugs," Leung said. "So we’re like, OK, well, obviously you can’t test this in humans. But we can try to do this in mice."

items: Generic Ozempic is now about $100 a month across the country. Canadians are taking note
Health Canada approves 1st generic version of Novo Nordisk's Ozempic

blocks.text: Leung and his research team did exactly that, and found cycling overweight mice through GLP-1 use seemed to make the drugs less effective over time. Mice who started and stopped the drugs every two weeks struggled to lose weight compared to mice who stayed on GLP-1s for the entire months-long study.
Even after two months of consistent use at the end of the study period, the drug-cycling group remained 20 per cent heavier.
If that was happening to mice, Leung started to wonder: What’s actually happening inside the bodies of human patients stopping and starting these body-changing drugs?
Ozempic: the future of addiction treatment?
'Buyer beware' when using GLP-1s off-label
Dr. Sean Wharton sees that regularly in his own patients at the Wharton Medical Clinic for weight and diabetes management in Burlington, Ont.
"People are using it off-label often. Maybe they heard about something on the internet or on Facebook. And if they're using it in this manner off-label, then it’s … buyer beware," he said.
"Because I don't know what type of negative aspects could potentially happen. There could be mainly positive and no negative aspects, but we don't exactly know yet."

items: People regained weight, worsened heart health after stopping weight loss drugs: review
Health Canada warns about fake or unauthorized versions of GLP-1 drugs

blocks.text: Wharton stressed this growing class of drugs has clear benefits as a long-term treatment for obesity, which has a dangerous domino effect on other health issues, like inflammation and cardiovascular disease, when left untreated.
Research also suggests GLP-1s may help curb substance use disorders, cut the severity of sleep apnea or even reduce cancer risk.
Dr. Sean Wharton is an internal medicine specialist and clinical researcher in obesity medicine in Toronto. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

Yet increasingly, these drugs are moving from tested treatment into what Wharton calls the "aesthetic medicine space" for short-term use. And he says the benefits likely vanish when patients rush back off these drugs.

"If losing the weight was the reason why your metabolic condition — like your heart failure, your high blood pressure — got better, then regaining the weight usually means that that blood pressure is going to go back up."

items: Ozempic use, protein-maxxing driving up whey protein prices
We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains

blocks.text: Last year, one major research review concluded that the "magnitude and consistency" of these kinds of health effects "underscore the physiological consequences of [GLP-1] discontinuation."
A key need, according to that research team, was treatment guidelines to also address how to stop using the drugs.
What's the best way to go off these drugs?

GLP-1 pioneer Dr. Daniel Drucker agrees with that approach. In Toronto, he’s helping lead a randomized controlled trial — the gold standard of health-care research — to find out the best way for people to safely stop taking the drugs that he helped bring to the masses.

The research team, which includes Wharton and Drucker’s colleague and fellow endocrinologist Dr. Caroline Kramer, is recruiting patients for a 16-week-long study period where they’ll go through regular bloodwork and other metrics to gauge the impact of slowly tapering off a GLP-1 compared to abruptly stopping.

items: How do semaglutides or GLP1's work?

blocks.text: "We’re trying to answer a very simple question: If someone wants to know, can they come off the GLP-1 medicines, what is the best way to do it?" Drucker told CBC News inside a lab at Mount Sinai Hospital.
"Pharmaceutical companies are not good at studying how to stop their medicine," Drucker said, "but we need to answer that question."

GLP-1 researchers Dr. Caroline Kramer, left, and Dr. Daniel Drucker are studying the best way to stop using these blockbuster drugs through a trial based out of Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto. (Lauren Pelley/CBC)

Drucker is among those who sees huge potential for GLP-1s as a way to reduce the dire impacts of obesity — a public health crisis so widespread that just this year, the World Health Organization released its first-ever guidelines to manage obesity starting from childhood.

But tackling long-term medical issues usually requires long-term treatment, he stressed. When you discontinue minoxidil for hair regrowth, for example, hair loss restarts. If you suddenly stop taking statins, cholesterol spikes fast. Why would GLP-1s be any different?

"There is a lot of stigma around staying on a medicine to control your body weight for long periods of time, but we would never have anyone question if they had MS or Crohn's or hypertension or high cholesterol," Drucker said.

"I could list at least 125 diseases where you take the medication for the rest of your life to control the disease, but for some reason with the GLP-1 medicine, people think, well, you should be able to do this yourself."
Short-term use may 'cause more harm than good'
Kramer said there really hasn’t been research to help show if the cardiovascular benefits of being on a GLP-1 can be maintained by gradually tapering off rather than quickly stopping.
The team will also be watching for symptoms and adverse events, given there can be a range of side-effects from common stomach upset to acute pancreatitis to rare reports of vision loss.

items: What does thin mean in the age of GLP1s?
Why cheaper weight loss drugs could be a 'gamechanger' for Canadians

blocks.text: Kramer's advice for Canadians who want to do a short-term stint on a weight-loss drug before her team’s results come in?
"Patients who want to shed, like, three pounds because, ‘I have a wedding in two weeks’ … that is not what the medications were meant for," she said.
"If you are thinking of taking a medication without the proper assessment over a short term … it may cause more harm than good."

articles.title: Major Chinese brands drop Mbappé as backlash grows over Mao joke
articles.summary: He allegedly said his "favourite meme" is "the one where they put my face on a Chinese dictator".

blocks.text: Even China's foreign ministry has weighed in, with spokesperso Lin Jian: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
Neither Mbappé nor the The Bridge have commented on this yet.

It's unclear when the interview was broadcast but Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments on Monday night in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".

A backlash quickly ensued online, with some users criticising Mbappé – who is hugely popular in China and has big endorsements - of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," read another comment on Weibo.

Mao founded Communist China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s. His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.

His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the Chinese Communist Party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
Given how Mao is regarded to this day in China, the may seem unsurprising to many.

The backlash is still growing. Chinese state broadcaster, CCTV, is suspending La Liga matches, according to The Paper. And some reports claim t 's state broadcaster CCTV's news apps no longer have content related to the French striker.
The Chinese brands have not explicitly said why they were terminating the contract but referred to hurt sentiments.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng, said: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
Given brands have not mentioned the controversial clip, some users on social media are also asking what exactly Mbappé had said or done that was offensive.

Mbappé, who made his debut for Real Madrid in August 2024, has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the football world because of his influence and control over club and international football operations.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches. Some say the incident reinforced his "dictator" portrayal.
The nickname has also made Mbappé the subject of many memes online.

France team-mate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup by calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.

In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveals a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life," he had said.

articles.title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions
articles.summary:
Italian army removes and defuses 250 explosives encased in ice for more than 100 years after hikers’ sightings

A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this…

blocks.text: A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.
The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.
The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.

blocks.caption: Soldiers from Italian army’s Julia Alpine brigade at work. Photograph: Julia Alpine brigade

blocks.text: More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.

They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.
It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.

blocks.caption: A soldier with some of the munitions recovered.  Photograph: Julia Alpine brigade

blocks.text: “It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.

“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”
The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.

Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.
after newsletter promotion

A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.

The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.
A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.
The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.
Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.
The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.
Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.
“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.
“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”

articles.title: 'I would do it again' - Kaepernick reflects on price of protest, 10 years on
articles.summary: In his first interview with BBC Sport since taking the knee for the first time, Colin Kaepernick reflects on his journey.

blocks.text: "I knew the protest could potentially cost me my career...I would absolutely do it again."
Ten years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status, but which he believes led to his exile from the sport he loved, Colin Kaepernick insists he has no regrets.
It was September 2016 when NFL star Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem before a match as a peaceful protest against racial injustice and police brutality.
It proved both inspirational and divisive.

In his first interview with BBC Sport, Kaepernick reflects on his journey; his pride at seeing England footballers take the knee, athlete activism, the relationship between sport and politics, and the price he paid for being a figurehead for the civil rights movement.
The former quarterback says he decided to protest despite suspecting it could risk his career.
"History shows us…that is a reality for athletes", he says.

"We also see this in broader movements, going well beyond costing someone their career, and costing people their lives. We see Malcolm X assassinated, we see MLK [Martin Luther King] assassinated, so the consequences are real."

Having initially sat to raise awareness of the plight of black people in the US, Kaepernick first knelt during the Star-Spangled Banner before his San Francisco 49ers team played a pre-season game. It was an act he would repeat before 11 regular-season contests that year.

At the time, he said he could not stand up for - and show pride in - a flag "for a country that oppresses black people and people of colour", adding: "This is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way."
His stance against racial inequality was seen as heroic by many, inspiring other NFL players to follow suit. But there was also condemnation from those who said it was disrespectful to the military.
Those dissenting voices included Donald Trump - then a presidential candidate.

Trump described the act as "a terrible thing" and unpatriotic. He even suggested Kaepernick should find another country to live in, adding players who refused to stand for the national anthem should be fired.
The NFL said it would fine teams whose players did not stand.
Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers in March 2017, though the club's management later said he would have been released regardless.
Despite leading the 49ers to the 2013 Super Bowl, and throwing 16 touchdowns in his final season, one of the most talented quarterbacks in the sport never found a new team.

Speaking from New York, Kaepernick says he anticipated the reaction to taking the knee. "What I couldn't have predicted was the people who would show up for me in significant ways, and also the people who worked against me and against the movement," he adds.
Kaepernick eventually filed a grievance against NFL team owners, who he believed had conspired not to hire him because of his protests, reaching a financial settlement in 2019.

That year, the NFL arranged a private workout for Kaepernick, but he chose not to attend, instead holding his own session elsewhere to allow media to be present. Hopes of a comeback never materialised.
The NFL later admitted it was "wrong for not listening to players earlier", and encouraged "all to speak out and peacefully protest".
Following the murder of George Floyd while in police custody in Minneapolis in 2020, taking the knee became a feature of Black Lives Matter protests, and widespread across sport.
England's men's and women's football teams were among those to follow suit.
"That was a surprising moment for me," says Kaepernick.

"I did think about the protest going beyond the US and how that may show up in other countries. To be able to see the national teams going out and protesting, it was humbling. I was happy that they were doing it.
"I also know there's still a lot of work to be done within racism in the UK and more broadly. And this is a global challenge that we are collectively fighting against.
"I was very excited to be able to see players actively calling that out, and willing to begin taking action towards addressing it."
Despite keeping a relatively low profile for most of the past decade, Kaepernick remains a standard-bearer for the civil rights movement.

But while surveys suggest the vast majority of professional athletes intend to use their social media channels to raise awareness about racial injustice, external, he accepts the momentum behind athlete activism seems to have slowed in recent years.
It was notable that several players across five clubs chose to remain standing when Premier League players took the knee as part of October's No Room for Racism campaign.

Anti-discrimination campaign group Kick It Out told BBC Sport the gesture "still has value in raising awareness of the structural inequalities that exist in football and society", but added it could "understand the reasons players might become frustrated with the pace of change".
Reports of discrimination received by the charity more than doubled in the past five years, reaching record levels last season.
"I think we're in a moment that demands protests more than ever," says Kaepernick.

"Why I think protests are not as loud right now [is] because of the concerted efforts that have been taken by organisations like the NFL, like the Trump administration, and corporate entities following along and capitulating in that process.
"While those things are happening, I think the reality of the state of the US, and more broadly the world, demands that we show up in a more significant way."
Kaepernick is all too familiar with how polarising it can be to take a political stand in sport.

Opponents of taking the knee have claimed it is a political and divisive statement, and that rather than demonstrating backing for the Black Lives Matter movement, it has shown support for the organisation of the same name.

In 2018, critics encouraged people to destroy Nike goods after the sportswear giant used Kaepernick as the face of an advertising campaign featuring the caption 'Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.'
So what does he say to those who argue that sport and politics should be kept apart?
"They ring hollow and feel very hypocritical, because politics is inherently part of sports," he says.

"We see within [American] football, we see taxpayers funding NFL stadiums. We see our NFL owners going out and supporting political candidates... so to try to position this as if sports aren't political, in many ways feels just laughable to me, and disconnected.

"Now, where the question comes in for people is: 'We don't want the athletes to be political. Everything around them can be political, but the athletes themselves, we don't want them to have a voice in the politics, because that interrupts our entertainment and our ability to disconnect.' For me, that's where society has a challenge with it."

Having encountered significant opposition from high-profile athletes during his first term, Trump seems to have encountered less challenge from the world of sport during his second, notably becoming the first sitting US president to attend the Super Bowl.
He has also appeared at golf's Ryder Cup, and the finals of football's Club World Cup and World Cup, though he was also booed when attending the NBA Finals in New York in June.

"It ties into the conversation of 'are sports political?' when he is going out and actively trying to use them to gain favour and popularity", says Kaepernick, adding that Fifa's controversial decision to award the US President its inaugural 'Peace Prize' last year was "regrettable".

"The part that I think is great to see is when he's showing up to these events and getting booed by the crowd, which speaks to the political environment that he's created, that the majority of the country does not agree with…when it comes to sports, people need to continue to respond accordingly."

Now 38, Kaepernick has published a memoir titled The Perilous Fight, detailing his childhood in California having been adopted by a white family, encountering racism, and his education and evolution. "People saw the moment. But they didn't see the years that made it possible", he says. "The questions about who I was; the injustices I could no longer ignore; the voices of those who came before me that I carried into that stadium...When I took a knee, it wasn't a sudden act. It was the result of years of becoming."
So how did he find the process of reliving that journey?
"Are there moments that are challenging going back to? Yes. But I hope that insight helps other people navigate situations...that helps them move forward or helps them to go accomplish things."
Kaepernick also supports community organisations via his Know Your Rights education campaign, is a philanthropist, and has written a number of children's books.
Even now, he maintains the fitness regime he had during his time at the 49ers, just in case an unlikely opportunity to resume his NFL career arises.
Kaepernick may not have thrown a ball in anger for almost a decade, but he is widely regarded as one of the most significant athletes in modern history.

The way he used his platform to promote change has been compared to legendary boxer Muhammad Ali's support of the anti-war movement, and US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos giving the Black Power Salute at the 1968 Olympics.
"To even be in the same conversation with the likes of [them], is extremely humbling," he says. "But more importantly, I just try to stay focused on the work.

"What can we do to help people? And how do we collectively move forward as a society? And, ultimately, how we build a society that works for everybody. That feels like a very simple principle that has been lost.

"I know in the US specifically, we have a lot of work to do there. I hope we begin taking the steps to get back to a place where we are actually addressing people's needs. And create a society that is equitable for everyone."

articles.title: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar
articles.summary: Donald Trump heads into the US midterm elections with an issue similar to his political foe Joe Biden.

blocks.text: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar
Image source, Getty Images
US President Donald Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden
ByMichelle Fleury
New York business correspondent
The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.
It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.
Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.
During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices.
"When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.
Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.
Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.
Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high.

The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.

The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.
Numbers only tell part of the story

US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.
Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.
Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".
Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told", external, arguing that "nobody is getting fired".
But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising.
Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%.
That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy.
Same language, different meanings
For Democrats, the dynamic feels familiar.
Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things.
"When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says.
"When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently

blocks.text: Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently
The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day.
Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators.
"You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says.
That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's.
The Trump effect
Biden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks.
Trump has less room to do that.
Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran.
"The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans.
"It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."
Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.
A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US households

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US households
The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.
Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.

The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.
Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress.
The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.
Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.
If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

articles.title: Albanese promises ‘swift response’ on MP safety as he mulls panic buttons for politicians
articles.summary:
Senator Fatima Payman also criticises former colleagues over lack of staffing given to her office

Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and…
articles.byline: Josh Butler and Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and floated the provision of duress alarms for electorate offices, saying politicians and their staff have put up with threats for too long.

The prime minister’s pledge to the Labor partyroom came hours after senator Fatima Payman again slammed her former government colleagues over the lack of staffing given to her office, controversially asking: “Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office?”

MPs across the political divide have spoken forcefully of the need for more protection for their offices after the alleged attack on the Indi MP last week, raising alarm about threats and violence directed to their staff. Politicians are also revealing the scale of abuse, online and offline, directed toward them, including death and rape threats.

In the first Labor partyroom meeting since the alleged attack, Albanese gave a long address, saying this week “must be a turning point” for civil discourse and how threats are responded to. He also conceded there needed to be more investment in security and safety for politicians.
Albanese said MPs have had to “put up with the threat environment for too long”, that the government “need to do more”, and “more can and should be done”.
“You’ve all dedicated so much to the safety of others in the workplace. I’m determined to make sure we do everything for your safety and the safety of your staff as well,” he said.

Albanese did not give specifics, but promised a “swift government response” on safety, and noted numerous MPs had raised the prospect of receiving duress alarms, or panic buttons, to alert authorities of a safety incident. This was among a “series of options” under consideration.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also told the meeting that the government was looking at safety at polling booths around election time.

Government sources said numerous changes were being considered, with a fulsome response and proposal likely to be revealed in coming days. MPs have raised a wide range of concerns, including greater security and hardening of their electoral offices, better communication with federal police, and resources for security at their private homes like CCTV and lighting – all options understood to be under consideration.
An ongoing review into commonwealth workplaces will also be expedited by Labor, with recommendations specifically about safety and security to be delivered soon.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told his MPs in a Coalition partyroom meeting of ongoing conversations with the government about personal safety and the importance of getting it right, but did not raise any specific proposals.
Payman speaks out

Payman, who quit Labor in 2024 to sit on the crossbench, on Monday night lashed out at the prime minister for not responding to a request for additional staff in line with other independent political offices.
after newsletter promotion

The prime minister has discretion over the allocation of personal staff, which are typically more senior advisers. All politicians receive electoral office staff, but Payman has zero advisers while 16 other crossbench MPs and senators shared 30 advisers, according to an internal document tabled in the hearing.

In a Senate estimates hearing, Payman questioned minister Don Farrell whether the staff allocation shortfall was due to Albanese having a personal gripe with her, claiming her staff were severely overworked.

“If [Albanese] cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you [Farrell] and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out,” she said.
“Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office? To me? For him to take our request seriously?”
Farrell and other Labor senators in the hearing strongly rejected the insinuation, but Payman refused to withdraw the comments when asked until her staffing request was dealt with.

Payman told Guardian Australia last week there had been a massive increase in the number of death threats and hate comments since 2024 when she defected from Labor. Payman said her office manager had opened mail last year containing human faeces, resulting in a biohazard team having to respond.

“We had all these people in hazmat suits come through [the office],” she said. “The trauma that that inflicts on my staff members is horrible. No office or no worker should ever have to deal with that kind of crap.”

articles.title: Israel election live: polls open in most consequential vote in country’s history
articles.summary: Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority, with Gadi Eisenkot the leading opposition contender

blocks.text: Polls open in elections for Israeli parliament

Hello and welcome to our coverage of the Israeli elections. Polls have opened in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, Israel’s subsequent destruction of Gaza, and the launch of its war with the US against Iran.

Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority in the 120-seat Knesset, but the opposition bloc will probably also fall short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

For Netanyahu, 76, who has led the most far-right government in Israel’s history, the stakes are both political and personal. He is on trial for corruption in three separate cases, despite interventions from Donald Trump, who called for a pre-emptive pardon in the long-running saga and even wrote to Israeli president Isaac Herzog on Netanyahu’s behalf. The cases are ongoing.

blocks.caption: Ballot boxes are set up at a school in Tel Aviv. Photograph: Nir Keidar/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: It was on Netanyahu’s watch that Hamas militants broke out from Gaza three years ago to kill nearly 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, on the deadliest day in Israel’s history. This election is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership since those attacks.

The IDF’s globally condemned assault on Gaza, which has killed at least 75,000 people and been deemed a genocide by a UN commission, academics, legal scholars and Israeli and international rights groups, has left Israel a pariah on the world stage.

Three years of regional conflict followed the 7 October attacks, including this year’s war on Iran, which sparked an ongoing global energy crisis and has killed thousands of people, mainly in Lebanon and Iran.

blocks.caption: A man looks at the wreckage of an Iranian missile that landed near the West Bank city of Jericho in June. Photograph: Mahmoud Illean/AP

blocks.text: What is more, under Netanyahu’s government there has been an unprecedented, aggressive surge of deadly extremist settler violence to bolster Israeli control in the occupied West Bank, as settler militants and their political backers – who have propped up Netanyahu’s government – exploited their seat at the cabinet table and expanded with impunity.

Indeed, settlement expansion has been a key feature of Netanyahu’s re-election campaign. However, it is also a driving force behind Israel’s growing international isolation, with many of its traditional allies condemning “settler terrorists” and announcing plans to impose sanctions.
Key events

34m agoPolls open in elections for Israeli parliament

blocks.text: Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main challenger in Tuesday’s elections, has already been out greeting voters at a polling station in Ofakim, in Israel’s south.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot visits a polling station in Ofakim. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP

blocks.text: The former army chief of staff spent four decades rising through the ranks of Israel’s military. He now leads the largest opposition party – Yashar.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot greets voters. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP

blocks.text: Explainer: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

blocks.caption: Emma Graham-Harrison

blocks.text: Emma Graham-Harrison
In Jerusalem

Israel is holding its first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, the deadliest day in the country’s history, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians.
Since then Israel has pursued a war of annihilation in Gaza, launched two inconclusive wars with Iran, and intensified a campaign of state-backed ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank.

Domestically the coalition formed by Benjamin Netanyahu has taken aim at democratic institutions, including the supreme court. Many Israelis have described this election as the most consequential in their country’s history.
Here, Emma runs through everything you need to know – from the key players and issues, to when we can expect the results:

articles.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
articles.summary:
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in…

blocks.text: Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.

The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.

The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.

The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.

“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.

The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.

As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.

But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.

“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.

blocks.caption: Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.

Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.

On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.

China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.

This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

articles.title: Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission
articles.summary: Around 2,000 people remain stranded in the city of Oleshky, facing severe shortages of food and medicine. The Russian-occupied town has been devastated by fighting and flooding since Moscow's…

image.caption: Ukrainian authorities have used drones to deliver food and medicine to residents stranded in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky [FILE: September 12, 2026]Image: 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia and Ukraine began a localized ceasefire early Tuesday to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
Both sides confirmed that the truce took effect at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT), following an agreement brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had stopped shelling in the Kherson sector to prepare for the humanitarian operation.
Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets also confirmed that Kyiv was observing the agreement.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
However, it could not be independently verified whether fighting had decreased.
What is the humanitarian situation in Oleshky?

Around 2,000 people, including up to 50 children, remain trapped in Oleshky, according to Ukrainian and US estimates. The town had about 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The United Nations says residents face severe shortages of food and medicine. Mines and drone attacks have made it difficult for them to leave.

blocks.caption: International media have limited access to Oleshky, making it difficult to independently assess conditions in the town [FILE: September 22, 2026]Image: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former residents told news agency AFP earlier this year that people remaining in the town were starving, sometimes hunting pigeons or surviving on food grown in their gardens.
"They've forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there's not even flour left," said Olga, who was in contact with two families still in Oleshky.
Oleshky lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson.

blocks.caption: Floodwaters submerged large parts of Oleshky in June 2023 after the collapse of the Kakhovka dam on the Dnipro River [FILE: June 10, 2023]Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russian troops captured the town during the first days of the invasion in 2022. It suffered further destruction in June 2023 when the collapse of the Kakhovka dam caused widespread flooding.
What role did Melania Trump play in the ceasefire?
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had helped secure the agreement after holding talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine.
Her office said the first lady had also met United Nations officials who briefed her on conditions in Oleshky.
Announcing the agreement on Friday, Trump said civilian officials from both countries would visit residents to assess their needs.

blocks.caption: US first lady Melania Trump has taken on an unusually prominent diplomatic role in efforts to address the humanitarian crisis in Ukraine [FILE: October 19, 2026]Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Doctors, food, drinking water and medicine are expected to reach the town before evacuation corridors are opened.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing residents from leaving, an allegation Moscow denies.
Neither side has provided details about who will monitor the ceasefire. Reports have also differed over its duration, with one account saying it could last through Saturday.
What happened in Kyiv after the ceasefire began?
Russian missile attacks continued elsewhere in Ukraine as the localized ceasefire began.
Explosions shook Kyiv shortly after 3 a.m. local time Tuesday, according to witnesses, while air raid alerts sounded across several regions.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attacks had damaged the Southern Bridge and associated subway infrastructure. City authorities said traffic on the bridge had been suspended.

blocks.caption: Buildings in Kyiv were damaged by Russian missile strikes, which also left several people dead or injuredImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Monday, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 10 others, including students at a dormitory. Further attacks caused casualties in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after the attacks.
Could the Oleshky ceasefire help revive Ukraine peace talks?
The limited truce in Oleshky comes ahead of another round of US-mediated peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, expected in November.
Negotiations have been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.

blocks.caption: The last trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US took place in Geneva in February 2026, ending without a breakthrough [FILE: February 17, 2026]Image: Yekaterina Chesnokova/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: Previous attempts to establish ceasefires have repeatedly failed amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine.
More than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed, while millions have been forced to flee their homes.
